To clothe or adorn.
d.x: We will attire him in fine clothing so he can make a good impression.

attire.e: The verb is from Middle English atyren, atiren, from Old French atirier (“to equip”), from a- + tire (“rank”), akin to German Zier (“ornament”) and Old Norse tírr (“glory, renown”). The noun is from Middle English atir, from the verb.

d.g: The position of the body or way of carrying oneself.
d.x: The ballet dancer walked with a graceful attitude.

d.g: A disposition or state of mind.
d.x: Don't give me your negative attitude.

d.g: Unpleasant behavior.
d.x: He doesn't take attitude from anybody.

d.g: The orientation of a vehicle or other object relative to the horizon, direction of motion, other objects, etc.
d.x: The airliner had to land with a nose-up attitude after the incident.

attitude.e: From French attitude, from Italian attitudine (“attitude, aptness”), from Medieval Latin aptitūdō (“aptitude”) and actitūdō (“acting, posture”), from Latin aptō and actitō. Doublet of aptitude.

d.g: British statesman and leader of the Labour Party who instituted the welfare state in Britain (1883-1967)
A lawyer; one who advises or represents others in legal matters as a profession.
d.x: “Conflicting out” attorneys is the way a husband will make sure his wife doesn't hire any of the most aggressive lawyers in town.

d.g: An agent or representative authorized to act on someone else's behalf in accordance with that person's instructions.
d.x: Near-synonyms: agent, proxy, representative

d.g: One such who practised in the courts of the common law.
A solicitor.

attorney.e: From Middle English attourne, from Old French atorné, past participle of atorner, atourner, aturner (“to attorn”), in the sense of "one appointed or constituted".

d.g: The office or profession of an attorney.

attorneyship.e: English attorney Proto-Germanic *skapjaną Proto-Germanic *-skapiz Proto-West Germanic *-skapi Old English -sċiepe Middle English -schipe English -ship English attorneyship From attorney + -ship.

d.g: An SI unit of time equal to 10⁻¹⁸ seconds. Symbol: as
d.x: Meronyms: quectosecond < rontosecond < yoctosecond < zeptosecond

attosecond.e: English atto- English second English attosecond From atto- + second.

d.g: an entertainer who attracts large audiences
The tendency to attract.
d.x: The Moon is held in its orbit by the attraction of the Earth's gravity.

d.g: The state of being attractive.
d.x: I can't resist his attraction.

d.g: An event, location, or business that has a tendency to draw interest from visitors, and in many cases, local residents.
d.x: The new mall should be a major attraction.

d.g: The sacrifice of pieces in order to expose the enemy king.

d.g: The state of being attractive or engaging.
The result of being attractive.

d.g: Something which attracts.
A set of points or states to which a dynamical system evolves after a long enough time. That is, points that get close enough to the attractor remain close even if slightly disturbed.
A characteristic or quality of a thing.
d.x: His finest attribute is his kindness.

d.g: An object that is considered typical of someone or some function, in particular as an artistic convention.
d.x: The eagle and the bolt of lightning are attributes of Jove.

d.g: A word that qualifies a noun.
That which is predicated or affirmed of a subject; a predicate; an accident.

attribute.e: Latin attributusbor. English attribute Borrowed from Latin attributus.

d.g: The act of attributing something.
An explicit or formal acknowledgment of ownership or authorship.
d.x: The attribution of the quote is widely regarded as dubious.

d.g: A legal doctrine by which liability is extended to a defendant who did not actually commit the tortious or criminal act.

attribution.e: From Middle French attribution, from Latin attributio.

d.g: Grinding down or wearing away by friction.
The wearing of teeth due to their grinding.
A gradual reduction in number.
A gradual, natural reduction in membership or personnel, as through injury, incapacitation, retirement, resignation, or death.

attrition.e: 15th century, from Middle English attricion, attricioun, from Middle French attricion, attrition and its etymon, Latin attrītiō (“a rubbing against”), from the verb attrītus, past participle of atterō (“to wear”), from ad- (“to, towards”) + terō (“to rub”). By surface analysis, attrit + -ion.

d.g: The condition of being atypical
Alternative spelling of atomize.
To separate or reduce into atoms.
To make into a fine spray.
d.x: Near-synonyms: aerosolize, vaporize

d.g: To fragment; to break into small pieces or concepts.
d.x: Near-synonyms: anatomize, analyze, scrutinize

d.g: To deprive of community and political capital.
d.x: Near-synonym: disunite

d.g: To make reparation, compensation, amends or satisfaction for an offence, crime, mistake or deficiency.
d.x: He tried to atone for his mistakes by working harder.

d.g: To absolve (someone else) of wrongdoing, especially by standing as an equivalent.

atone.e: From atone (“reconciled”), from Middle English atone, attone, atoon (“agreed”, literally “at one”), equivalent to at + one. Compare Latin adūnō (“to unite, make one”) for the similar formation. Regarding the different phonological development of atone and one, see the note in one.

d.g: To fasten, to join to (literally and figuratively).
d.x: You need to attach the carabiner to your harness.

d.g: To adhere; to be attached.
d.x: The great interest which attaches to the mere knowledge of these facts cannot be doubted.

d.g: To include an attachment with a communication (especially an email or other electronic communication).
d.x: I've attached the contract to this email.

d.g: To come into legal operation in connection with anything; to vest.
d.x: Dower will attach.

attach.e: From Middle English attachen, from Old French atachier, variant of estachier (“bind”), derived from estache (“stick”), from Frankish *stakkā, *stakō (“stick”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“pole, bar, stick, stake”). Doublet of attack. More at stake, stack. Displaced native Old English þīedan.

d.g: To come to or reach (a place) by motion or progression.
d.x: Canaan he novv attains, I ſee his Tents / Pitcht about Sechem, and the neighbouring Plaine / Of Moreh; […]

d.g: To arrive at (a certain age or time, condition or state, etc.); to reach.
d.x: Night hangs vpon mine eyes, my Bones vvould reſt, / That have but labour'd, to attaine this houre.

d.g: To gain (a desired result or other objective) through effort; to accomplish, to achieve.
d.x: To attain such a high level of proficiency requires hours of practice each day.

d.g: To arrive at a certain condition or state, etc.

attain.e: The verb is derived from Middle English atteinen, atteynen (“to achieve, attain; to be adequate or sufficient; to affect; to come or get to (a place), reach; to corrupt, taint; to overcome, overpower; to overtake; to succeed; to tamper with; (law) to bring to justice, punish”), from ataign-, a stem of Anglo-Norman atai …

d.g: A wound on the leg of a horse caused by a blow.

attaint.e: From Middle English atteinte, from Old French ateint, past participle of ateindre; in some senses influenced by taint.

d.g: To temper by adjusting relative quantities, or blending qualities.
To mitigate, assuage.

attemper.e: From Middle English attempren, from Old French atemprer (French attremper), from Latin attemperare. Doublet of attemperate.

d.g: To care for (someone requiring attention); specifically, of a doctor, nurse, etc.: to provide professional care to (someone).
d.x: The fift [beadsman] had charge ſick perſons to attend, / And comfort thoſe, in point of death vvhich lay; […]

d.g: To wait on (someone or their instructions) as an attendant, servant, etc.; also (specifically of a gentleman-in-waiting or lady-in-waiting to a member of royalty), to accompany (someone) in order to assist or wait upon them; to escort.
d.x: Servants attend the king day and night.

d.g: To be present at (an event or place) in order to take part in some action or proceedings; also, to regularly go to (an event or place).
d.x: Children must attend primary school.

d.g: To take action with respect to (someone, or something such as a concern, problem, or task); to deal with, to handle.

attend.e: PIE word *h₂éd From Middle English attenden, atenden (“to devote oneself (to a task, etc.); to pay attention to (something), to look after; to consider (something); to expect or look forward to (something); to intend to do (something); to help or serve (someone), attend upon; to take care of (something)”), from Old Fre …

d.g: To affirm to be correct, true, or genuine.
d.x: When will the appraiser attest the date of the painting?

d.g: To certify by signature or oath.
d.x: You must attest your will in order for it to be valid.

d.g: To certify in an official capacity.
To supply or be evidence of.
d.x: Her fine work attested her ability.

attest.e: PIE word *tréyes Borrowed from Middle French attester, from Latin attestor (“to witness to, bear witness”), from at-, combining form of ad (“to”) + testor (“to bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”).

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard form of attitudinize.
d.x: In every line that he wrote Cicero was attitudinising for posterity, or reflecting on the effect of his conduct upon his interests or his reputation.

attitudinise.e: From Italian attitudine + -ise, from Latin aptitūdin- + -ise, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -ise.

d.g: To cause (someone or something) to assume an attitude or pose; to pose, to posture.
d.x: In Greenwich, there were many gravelled walks, unshrubbed except for the nurses who dotted them, silent and attitudinized as trees.

d.g: To give the appearance of, or make a show of, (something) by assuming an affected or exaggerated attitude.
To assume an attitude or pose, especially one which is affected, exaggerated, or unnatural; to posture, to posturize; also, to excessively practise adopting attitudes or poses.
d.x: He had a great averſion to geſticulating in company. He called once to a gentleman vvho offended him in that point, "Don't attitudeniſe."

d.g: To create art, speak, or write in a manner which assumes affected, exaggerated, or unnatural attitudes.
d.x: In every line that he wrote Cicero was attitudinising for posterity, or reflecting on the effect of his conduct upon his interests or his reputation.

attitudinize.e: From Italian attitudine + -ize, from Latin aptitūdin- + -ize, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -ize.

d.g: To transfer one's obligations from one person to another person.
To consent to the transfer of one's obligations as tenant under a lease to a new landlord.
To acknowledge the jurisdiction of (a particular court) over one's dispute.

attorn.e: From Middle English attournen, from Old French atorner (“designate”), from a- (“to”) + torner (“turn”).

d.g: To pull toward without touching.
d.x: A magnet attracts iron filings.

d.g: To draw by moral, emotional or sexual influence; to engage or fix, as the mind, attention, etc.; to invite or allure.
d.x: to attract admirers

d.g: To incur.
d.x: Using the minibar in a hotel room attracts additional charges.

attract.e: From Latin attractus, past participle of attrahere (“to draw to, attract”), from ad (“to”) + trahere (“to draw”).

d.g: To bring into musical accord.
To tune (an instrument).
To bring into harmony or accord.
d.x: By meditating, I try to attune myself to the greater cosmos.

d.g: To fill with music.

attune.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad-bor. English ad- English tune English attune From ad- + tune.
